text:
The deal is being developed as Prime Minister Keir Starmer and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung prepare for the G7 leaders’ summit.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LONDON — Britain and South Korea are moving towards sealing a critical minerals partnership as the two countries look to reduce their dependence on Chinese supply chains.

The deal has been identified as one area where Prime Minister Keir Starmer can make progress at the G7 summit in France next week, according to an internal Whitehall briefing seen by POLITICO.

London also hopes to prioritize talks in Évian on a planned “nuclear fusion summit” with the U.S., according to a government official and two industry figures.

“There’s a discussion of a global fusion summit,” said one senior U.S. nuclear industry figure, granted anonymity to discuss the plans. “We are not sure of the scope of participants, but it is consistent with the Trump administration’s real focus on fusion.”

In September last year, both the U.S. and U.K. committed to a global fusion energy policy summit, co-hosted in the U.S. in 2026 — though no date or location has been announced yet.

Earlier this year, the U.S. hosted more than 50 countries for an inaugural Critical Minerals Ministerial. On the sidelines of the meeting, the U.K. signed a bilateral pact with the Trump administration agreeing to pursue measures to diversify the minerals market and protect against Chinese economic coercion.

Critical minerals will be the focus of one of seven sessions convened by French President Emmanuel Macron at next week’s summit in Évian, which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung is expected to attend as a guest.

Starmer will attend the gathering of world leaders against a backdrop of domestic political turmoil as he seeks to shore up his position and demonstrate he is delivering on key pledges.

Both Korea and the U.K. have now finalized talks on a framework agreement to strengthen collaboration on critical minerals, said one diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the negotiations.

The pact builds on the clean energy partnership struck between South Korea and the U.K. under Rishi Sunak’s government in November 2023, where both sides committed to explore a deal to collaborate on research and innovation through greater information sharing.

South Korea, with more than 95 percent of its critical minerals imported from abroad, is particularly vulnerable to Chinese rare earth curbs. As a mega player in the electric vehicle and semiconductor industries, it is actively trying to play a bigger role in the processing part of the critical minerals supply chain.

The Korean government recently approved the reopening of a tungsten mine in Gangwon Province after more than 30 years. The critical mineral is used in steel, as well as missile and defense systems. When fully operational, it is estimated the mine will produce roughly 40 percent of global tungsten supply outside of China, according to operator Almonty Industries.

Both the U.K. and Korea are “key industrial countries and technology providers,” said Patrick Schroder, senior research fellow at the Environment and Society Centre at Chatham House.

“The U.K. and Korea have an important role to play in helping to build a more inclusive international minerals governance framework that addresses the current governance gap,” Schröder added.

But while the strategic partnership could strengthen supply chain security, it “can only achieve so much in a fragmented and highly competitive landscape,” he cautioned. “The UK and Korea should look beyond narrow access to critical minerals and support wider international cooperation on responsible production, circularity, transparency and shared data.”

A U.K. government spokesperson said: “Our Critical Minerals Strategy is leveraging Britain’s mineral wealth, attracting new investment and building more resilient supply chains.”

“Diversifying supply is central to our strategy, and we remain committed to working with countries in promoting responsible sourcing and high environmental and social standards to ensure we have the critical minerals that we need to make our supply chains ready for the future.”

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on the global fusion summit.

Warren Stephens also warns UK social media ban is “a little draconian from a freedom of speech point of view.”

The former mayor’s intervention offers one of the most revealing insights yet into his thinking on trade.

The health department said disclosure would “prejudice ongoing policy development, international relations and commercial interests.”

Varun Chandra will stay on as No. 10’s top business adviser and U.S. envoy.
